timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What's a SIEM? Sounds like something from Star Trek.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: SIEM stands for Security Information and Event Management. Think of it as a security camera system, but for your digital infrastructure. It collects logs from every server, firewall, and application.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Everything. And it correlates events to detect threats. A single failed login is nothing. But 1000 failed logins from different countries in 5 minutes? That's a brute-force attack, and SIEM catches it.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The challenge is tuning. Too many rules and you get alert fatigue. Target's SIEM detected their 2013 breach, but the team ignored the alerts. 40 million credit cards stolen.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So it's only useful if people pay attention?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. That's why SOC teams exist - Security Operations Centers. Their entire job is monitoring SIEM alerts and responding to incidents. It's a 24/7 operation.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The MITRE ATT&CK framework is used to map SIEM detections to specific attacker techniques. Each detection rule should map to at least one ATT&CK technique.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What are the popular SIEM tools?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Splunk is the industry leader, but it's expensive. Elastic SIEM, Microsoft Sentinel, and IBM QRadar are alternatives. For learning, set up an ELK stack with Suricata IDS.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain how SIEM works, give examples of detection rules, and discuss the challenges of SIEM tuning and alert fatigue.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I want to set one up for my home lab now.
